item.title: Democrats clinch historic House majority after a 330-vote recount win in North Carolina
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House on Sunday, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades. Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far , four more than the 40 they picked up in President Trump's first midterm in 2018. It's an election sweep unseen since 1992 for either party, creating not only vast opportunities for Democrats to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities . The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes following a recount, according to the North Carolina Board of Elections . "House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, wrote on X Sunday afternoon. The milestone in the 435-member House exceeded Democrats' own expectations, and they could still gain a few more seats with four other House races remaining outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff. Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority. The blue wave, or as some have called it, "blue tsunami," sets up a divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address the high cost of living while also confronting Mr. Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term. The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300. It presents opportunities and challenges ahead. In an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Jeffries repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?" Election rout creates a mandate to govern The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and war with Iran and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Mr. Trump. Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats in their House races, according to CBS News exit polls. This was the second straight election most voters told CBS News inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters also backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House. Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade. The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire. Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Mr. Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr. Trump for a third time. "This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol. The New York Democrat called the big numbers "a mandate for change." Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability. "Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said. For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr. Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?" The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality." A new generation of leaders After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver. Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition. "We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democratic Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus. Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994. Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power. "Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said. The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/democrats-historic-house-majority-since-1992/

item.title: NYC releases 84,000 more 9/11 records as portal tops 11 million visits
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Tribute in Light is illuminated on the skyline of lower Manhattan in New York City on Sept. 11, 2024. (LEONARDO MUNOZ/Getty Images) New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration released 84,000 more records Sunday on the city's response to the Sept. 11 attacks, pushing its public portal past 440,000 pages as unique visits topped 11 million. The batch is the third installment under a settlement with 9/11 Health Watch, an advocacy group created by the New York State AFL-CIO, and City Hall said more records will follow in the coming months. Mamdani's fiscal 2027 budget sets aside $34 million to build and maintain the portal. "More than 11 million visits and 440,000 pages later, our work is not finished," Mamdani said in a statement . Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal framed each release as a step toward answering when City Hall learned the air at ground zero could make people sick. The city counts its releases in records but measures the archive in pages. An October installment of 40,000 records lifted the total to more than 200,000 pages, up from roughly 170,000 at the portal's September launch . That first release included the so-called Harding Memo, an undated letter to Robert Harding, a deputy mayor under former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, that listed potential grounds for lawsuits against the city, including health advisories that sent people back into the area too soon. It also included the "68 boxes" of Department of Environmental Protection files that the city said went unlocated until 2025 despite repeated requests under the state's public records law. The releases have drawn pushback from Giuliani's camp. His spokesman, Ted Goodman, accused Mamdani in September of trying to score political points by blaming local officials rather than radical Islam, and Giuliani said the terrorists bore full responsibility while faulting the Environmental Protection Agency for declaring air samples safe, NBC New York reported . The disclosures followed a courtroom loss for the city. In a May 28 decision, Justice James G. Clynes of the New York State Supreme Court in Manhattan, the state's trial-level court, found the department had acted "arbitrarily and capriciously," meaning without a reasonable basis, in denying the group's records request, according to the settlement signed Sept. 2. The deal requires monthly meetings for a year to review how many documents and pages the city has posted, plus a log of records it located but withheld. Separately, the city's Department of Investigation, its internal watchdog agency, is examining what officials knew about post-9/11 air quality and when they knew it, in an inquiry mandated by the City Council, amNY reported . © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: 'Appetite for change': Van Hollen claims momentum in battle for Senate majority leader
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that “momentum is in our direction” in his bid for Senate majority leader. Asked directly how much support he had within the Democratic caucus, Van Hollen said the number is “north of 15” although it’s short of the 28 votes needed to win the leadership race against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Democratic senators and senators-elect will hold a vote in December to determine the next majority leader, a dominant role in shaping the party’s agenda and its response to the Trump administration. Van Hollen’s allies have sought to frame him as a leader who can push for change, while Schumer’s allies have argued that his leadership helped usher in historic Democratic wins across the country. Asked whether he believes he can secure enough votes, Van Hollen said yes. “Yes, because if you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change,” he said in the Sunday interview. “They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate.” Van Hollen also said he believes the Democratic Party is “on probation” and needs to earn Americans’ trust. “You don’t earn people’s trust by going back to business as usual,” he said. Van Hollen said he personally believes that the filibuster, which requires that most bills in the Senate need at least 60 votes to pass, “is an anti-democratic provision.” “But I also understand that the job of the majority leader is to work with the caucus,” he continued. “So we should set sort of standards and criteria for at what level of obstruction by Republicans — to root out political corruption, to move forward on voting rights — at what level will we consider alternatives?” he said, listing two major policy fights for which Democrats could potentially change the rules. One possibility, he said, is requiring a talking filibuster so that Republicans would have to show their opposition to popular proposals on the Senate floor. Van Hollen, who has been floated as a potential presidential candidate, also confirmed on “Meet the Press” that he will not run for president, even if he loses the leadership race. Van Hollen initially said he was “kicking the tires” on a presidential run, but after jumping in the Senate leadership race, he said he was not pursuing a presidential run anymore. “After I saw the scope of this victory, this call from the American people, my view is now we have to deliver, we have to earn people’s trust, and that would be my focus entirely,” he said. “So no, I’m not running for president in 2028.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/van-hollen-momentum-senate-majority-leader-schumer-election-rcna610669

item.title: Army invokes emergency powers to bypass court order and detonate lead in Iowa
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jack Queen and Jim Urquhart AUGUSTA, Iowa, Nov 22 (Reuters) - The US Army will detonate 68 barrels of a toxic lead explosive in Iowa this week on emergency legal powers that allow it to bypass a court order blocking the controversial plan, the Trump administration told a court this ‌weekend. The US Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the Army's environmental permit on Thursday after environmental groups sued to ‌halt the operation. The government said in Saturday night's filing that the Army plans to move forward without a permit by invoking an emergency munitions and explosives exception to federal environmental protection laws. Federal officials say the ​detonation must go forward within the next several days because a drop in temperature could destabilize the material and cause an uncontrolled explosion. "The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion," the Justice Department said in a court filing late on Saturday. The Army had previously postponed plans to detonate the degraded lead azide, an explosive used in military munitions, after public outcry by residents and farmers near Middletown, Iowa. The Justice Department said the Army would act by Tuesday, November ‌24. The Army later said in a post on ⁠X on Sunday the detonation would take place on Wednesday, November 25, "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced." The Army did not respond to a Reuters inquiry on Sunday about the precise timing of the detonation. "Additional details on this situation will ⁠be forthcoming," the Army said in its X post. DETAILS SOUGHT Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system. The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter filed the lawsuit challenging the detonation, arguing that the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 100 miles (160 km) ​north ​of the site, depending on weather conditions. Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs at the ​Iowa Environmental Council, told Reuters the Army should provide more details ‌about the timing of the detonation, where the plume is expected to travel, and what precautions people should take. “One of the pieces that especially raised our concerns was the lack of prior notice and the fact that many folks, including state officials, did not have any heads-up about this… There was not enough information being shared," Johannsen said. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment indoors or transport them to alternate locations. But farmers have told the environmental council that keeping livestock indoors is not a viable option, Johannsen said. In a statement on Thursday, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle ‌said the Army had determined with the US Environmental Protection Agency that a controlled detonation ​to dispose of the degraded lead was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public. Still, ​the Army advised people to avoid the affected area during the detonation and ​urged anyone who could not leave beforehand to stay indoors, close windows and doors and shut off heating and cooling systems that ‌bring in outside air. Residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch ​to remove any lead dust once the exposure ​period has ended, the Army said. “The early recommendations from the Army had a lot of people sort of with their jaws hanging open … There remain so many questions about mitigation and protection," Johannsen said. Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, said he planned to head west because he expected the plume ​would blow south through his town. "Anything but the bomb," Atwater ‌told Reuters outside his home, as a set of two green swings in his yard swayed in the wind. "It's just going to be a ​big problem." (Reporting by Jack Queen in New York and Jim Urquhart in Augusta, Iowa; additional reporting by Ashraf Fahim in Washington and Luc Cohen ​in New York; Editing by Sergio Non, Bill Berkrot, Stephen Coates and Lincoln Feast.) item.title: Rep. Virginia Foxx loses reelection bid after 11 terms in North Carolina
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx has been officially unseated by Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard in North Carolina after a recount — requested by Foxx — broke in Hubbard’s favor. The Associated Press called the election for Hubbard early Sunday afternoon. Hubbard, who lost to Foxx by 19 points two years ago, said in a statement that the incumbent had "graciously conceded." "Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," Hubbard wrote on social media. "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District." Hubbard's win marks the seventh seat Democrats flipped in the state this year despite Republican redistricting efforts last year. North Carolina will send 11 Democrats and three Republicans to Congress — a reversal of the 10-4 Republican majority voters elected in 2024. The Democratic win also notches the broader party an election-year record: Having secured 258 seats, the Democrats have won their largest share of House seats in a national election since the early '90s. Foxx had requested the recount in a letter to election officials on Nov. 17, when the margin between the two candidates was 331 votes. In her letter to the State Board of Election, Foxx cited a state law that allows candidates to request a recount when the margin of victory is less than 1 percent. Foxx was first elected in 2004. Now 83, she is finishing her 11th term and has already filed paperwork to run in the 2028 race. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/22/rep-virginia-foxx-loses-reelection-01180093

item.title: Jon Ossoff's decisive Senate win in Georgia fuels presidential buzz
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding reelection victory in Georgia is drawing renewed attention to his potential as a 2028 presidential contender, as election data shows how he assembled a broad coalition of voters in the pivotal presidential battleground state. Despite the growing speculation, Ossoff, 39, is for now dismissing the possibility of a White House bid. During a debate in October, Ossoff said he had "zero interest in running for president" in 2028. Some early polls place him at the top of a hypothetical 2028 primary field. A post-election Emerson College survey showed Ossoff with the support of 17% of respondents — narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom rounding out the top five. Ossoff has attracted interest from both centrists and progressives while delivering a decisive victory in a closely divided presidential battleground state. At Crooked Con, a primarily progressive gathering in Washington after the midterms, Ossoff received 38% of first-choice votes in its straw poll, ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg. "I think he would make an attractive presidential contender on the Democratic side," said Jerry Gonzalez, CEO of GALEO Impact Fund PAC, a Georgia-based Latino political action committee that endorsed Ossoff in his Senate race. "He is not afraid, he won't shy away from holding the Trump administration accountable, but in a way that works towards actually building coalitions to get something done." Democrats who can win statewide in conservative or swing states tend to be moderate, and that's true of Ossoff, too. "He comes across, and tries to present himself, as a moderate, and he talks about issues which moderate conservatives could get behind," said Charles Bullock, a longtime political science professor at the University of Georgia. "The issues he stresses are things which are within the broad mainstream of 'These would be good things.'" It's unclear how well a moderate would fare in the early nominating states. What is effective in a Georgia general election may be a tougher sell in a Democratic primary, where voters often reward ideological purity over swing-state caution. "Obviously, he's successful here in Georgia," Bullock said. "How would he play elsewhere? "I think what we will be seeing is preparation, maybe for a later run," Bullock speculated. Ossoff's record gives rivals on both flanks openings to attack: progressives have criticized his vote for the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and his reluctance to embrace "Medicare for All," while his votes to restrict certain weapons sales to Israel and his criticism of its military conduct in Gaza have drawn objections from some pro-Israel Democrats and donors. All of those issues are certain to be part of the 2028 primary contest. For example, Rep. Ro Khanna, another potential 2028 candidate, last week tried to restart the debate over universal healthcare. "Medicare for All means healthcare for everyone, like public school is free for every kid," Khanna wrote on X, arguing, "'Medicare for All who want it' is pablum. It's telling parents they have to pay for public school." In his reelection this month, Ossoff defeated GOP opponent Mike Collins by around 18 points, two years after President Trump defeated Harris by around two points in 2024. It was a much wider margin than his last Senate election, which he won by just over one percentage point. Powering Ossoff's win this year was a broad coalition of voters, including some swing constituencies that Democrats have struggled with in recent years, CBS News' exit polling shows. Ossoff maintained strong support among Black voters, winning 93% of the group, which make up almost one-third of the state's eligible voters according to Pew Research Center . He did not win the White voters who make up just over half of Georgia's electorate, but he did make significant inroads, winning 40% — after Harris had won just 28% two years earlier. He also notched some improvement in groups that have shifted hard against Democrats: He won 29% of White voters without college degrees (compared to Harris' 18%) and 19% of White evangelical or born-again Christian voters (compared to less than 10% for Harris). Ossoff also won men by nine points after Harris lost them by 13 points. Both Ossoff and Harris won younger Georgians, but Ossoff won them by a larger margin, securing 85% of voters ages 29 and under. Ossoff also split the 45-and-older vote roughly in half, while Harris lost that age group by a 15-point margin. And Ossoff made gains with Hispanics — a group that makes up less than 10% of Georgia's eligible voters but which has grown rapidly and has become a swing demographic that could decide a close race in the perennial battleground. In his reelection victory, he won around two-thirds of Latino voters, up seven points from Harris' performance two years earlier. A comparison of 19 Georgia precincts where at least 30% of active registered voters identify as Hispanic or Latino shows substantial Democratic improvement. Ossoff won those precincts by a combined 49 points in the two-candidate vote, compared with an eight-point advantage for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and an 18-point margin for fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022. The changes were significant in areas that had supported Mr. Trump just two years earlier. In six heavily Latino precincts in Whitfield County, the combined results shifted from a 12-point Trump advantage in 2024 to a 37-point Ossoff victory in 2026. Three similar precincts in Hall County shifted from an 11-point Trump edge to a 33-point Ossoff victory. Those figures reflect the voting behavior of entire precincts rather than individual Latino voters, and comparisons between presidential and midterm electorates are not exact. Still, they underscore how dramatically the environment changed in places with large Latino populations. Gonzalez attributed the shift in part to concerns over affordability and immigration enforcement, two issues he said weighed heavily on Latino voters in Georgia. "Things are really expensive," Gonzalez told CBS News. "The price and affordability were a big driving issue." He also pointed to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and its impact on Latino communities in Georgia. Ossoff has investigated allegations of abuses in federal immigration detention facilities as part of his Senate oversight work. Gonzalez also credited Ossoff's success among voters across the political spectrum to his accessibility and constituent outreach. "His office is accessible to all Georgians, and that's part of the reason why he won." In this wave election, Ossoff wasn't the only Democrat to pick up ground in the midterms. Latino and Black voters, men, voters without college degrees and younger voters moved back toward Democratic candidates nationwide, a reversal after all four groups had shifted rightward in 2024. In 2028, those groups could once again play a central role in both the Democratic Party's nominating process and the general election. States with large Black and Latino populations will lead the Democratic primary calendar after the party rearranged its schedule, and Ossoff, with his strong support from both groups, would likely stand to benefit if he were to decide to run. South Carolina — where Black Democratic voters have long played an influential role in choosing the party's presidential nominee — will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia. The DNC says approximately 4.2 million Latinos live across the six early nominating states, a major increase from the party's previous early-state lineup. In the general election, maintaining a strong lead with Black, Latino and younger voters — and preventing too much slippage among White and non-college-educated voters — will also be a core task for Democrats, as they seek to prevent the GOP's first non-Trump presidential candidate in over a decade from reassembling the Trump coalition. Though Ossoff says he doesn't plan a White House bid in 2028, his performance in Georgia has provided an early measure of what an electoral coalition for him could look like. "He has mentioned that he was focused on winning reelection, which he has done, so I think that gives him a little bit of latitude to think about it a little more seriously," Gonzalez said. item.title: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed says he's open to working with the Trump administration
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said Sunday that he’s open to working with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans, just weeks after the three men lobbed verbal attacks at each other during a tense campaign. Asked whether he intended to meet with the president or vice president soon, El-Sayed told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that “plans are in the works.” “As I said, I’m open to speaking with anybody. I’m the senator-elect for the state of Michigan. My people, the people in the state, elected me to serve them, and I’ll work with anyone who’s ready to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All,” El-Sayed added, repeating a refrain from his campaign. “I’m looking forward to those conversations about what we can do together, whether it’s with Democrats or Republicans.” Multiple times while campaigning for El-Sayed’s opponent, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, Trump labeled the then-Democratic Senate nominee a “ jihadist ” and referred to him by his middle name, “ Mohamed. ” El-Sayed accused the president and his allies of Islamophobia in the wake of these attacks. In his victory speech on election night, the senator-elect addressed the president directly, saying, “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator.” One of the key proposals from the senator-elect’s campaign for Senate was to pass a measure that would guarantee healthcare for Americans “from cradle to grave.” On Saturday, he engaged with Trump on social media with a post on X suggesting that new healthcare legislation could be named, “Trumpcare.” “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote , alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “Trumpcare” inscribed on it. The president later posted the image on his own social media account, but didn’t add his own comments. On Sunday, the vice president’s team confirmed that they were informed that El-Sayed is interested in meeting with Vance and that Vance’s office reached out to El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting. In an interview on Fox News on Saturday, Trump said he would be open to working with Democrats on healthcare, noting that their proposals have “good points” and “bad points.” In response to a request for comment on Sunday, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told NBC News, “As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” In Sunday’s “Meet the Press” interview, El-Sayed said he did see an opening to working with Trump, telling moderator Kristen Welker: “Well, the president signaled openness to the opportunity, and you know I played lacrosse growing up, and I was always taught that you play the ball, not the man. My job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country healthcare.” The senator-elect also clarified that while he supports “Medicare for All,” the specific proposal he’d like to see advance is one offering a public option for insurance. “What I’d like to see is somewhat like thinking about health insurance like public schools,” El-Sayed said. “Everybody is entitled to public schools. Some people send their kids to private schools, but the next day, if they wanted to, they could send their kids to public schools. Everybody is entitled to it. That’s how I’m thinking about public health insurance under Medicare for All. Everybody’s entitled.” “I think it’s about the guarantee and the security that it offers,” he added. item.title: Bay Area residents urged to avoid Thanksgiving travel as extreme flooding looms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Caltrans employees work to unclog drains in floodwater near Highway 101 freeway in San Francisco on Wednesday. (Benjamin Fanjoy / Getty Images) The California coast could see all-time-high sea levels this week, with officials warning of the potential for major seawater flooding of coastal neighborhoods. The San Francisco Bay Area faces an added threat because a strong storm will strike the region just as the highest tides so far this year arrive. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel, with the city still reeling from exceptional flooding from last week’s powerful rainstorm. Problems are also likely on the Southern California coast, where sea levels could be even higher than on Oct. 27, when records were shattered and homes and businesses were flooded in cities including Huntington Beach, Newport Beach, Long Beach, Redondo Beach and San Diego. The dangerous weather is being fueled by El Niño, hot ocean temperatures and unusually powerful king tides that are among the highest in two decades. Unlike Southern California, Northern California will also see a moderate-to-heavy rainstorm starting Tuesday, expected to whip up larger breaking waves and add to the potential for flooding. Even San Francisco International Airport and Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport are at risk of flooding, according to meteorologist Anamaria Navarrete of the National Weather Service’s Monterey office, which warned of “extreme coastal flooding” along the San Francisco Bay shoreline. “San Francisco could face a combination of exceptionally high tides, heavy rain and strong winds over the coming days,” the mayor said in a video posted on social media. “And our waterfront is expecting king tides, which are anticipated to bring the highest tide levels in San Francisco’s history. “This is a warning that I want everybody to take seriously. We want you to avoid unnecessary travel, especially around these peak tide periods that are coming,” Lurie said. The San Francisco Department of Emergency Management suggested avoiding unnecessary travel starting Monday afternoon through Wednesday; Marin County officials urged the same between 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day, especially in flood-prone areas. Crews were rushing to install emergency flood barriers along the bay shoreline, including at the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge toll plaza, where a “ Tiger Dam ” was installed. State transportation officials ordered the shutdown of the only vehicular route out of western Alameda to Oakland — the Posey Tube tunnel — starting Sunday night. And Marin County said people on the entire Tiburon Peninsula should consider leaving low-lying areas before the daily highest tide, starting Sunday through Black Friday, due to the flood risk. A motorist tries to navigate the 2300 block of Willow Street in Long Beach after heavy rains flooded the area on Thursday. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times) Set during the most powerful El Niño on record — and during a confluence of extremely high tides and a big storm — the all-time maximum sea level at the San Francisco tidal gauge at Crissy Field was set on Jan. 27, 1983, at 8.66 feet above the baseline (currently defined as the average daily lowest-water level observed between 1983 and 2001). As of Saturday morning, the prediction for the maximum sea level this week was 8.8 feet, but by Sunday morning, the prediction was adjusted downward to 8.6 feet. It’s still possible that sea levels could exceed 9 feet. “That is all dependent on how much storm surge that we get,” Navarrete said Saturday evening. “We can guarantee that we’ll have at least a foot to a foot and a half due to thermal expansion because of our warmer waters,” but it’s the level of storm surge that comes with the storm that’ll determine “if we are going to break records.” “Places that have rarely, or never, flooded before may be inundated,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said . It’s not rain falling from the sky that’s the main threat; it’s areas at risk of saltwater flooding from the ocean or the bay, he added. The rain itself isn’t expected to be as intense as last week’s historic rainfall that hit the Bay Area, which brought 3.2 inches to San Francisco in two days. This week’s storm could bring roughly 1 to 1.5 inches to San Francisco between Tuesday afternoon and Wednesday afternoon — still substantial and impactful because it’ll coincide with the king tides, Navarrete said. The king tides — influenced solely by the position of the moon and sun — are large because we’re near the peaks of what are known as the 18.6-year lunar node tidal cycle and the 4.4-year lunar perigee tidal cycle. Record-breaking ocean temperatures are also influencing the high sea levels, since hotter water takes up more volume. Southern California isn’t getting a major storm this week. Still, meteorologists warned that areas spared from hurricanes Marie and Rachel in early September and early October, and from high tides Oct. 27, could get hit with coastal flooding this week. In Orange and San Diego counties, forecasters with the National Weather Service warned of “extreme” risk from coastal flooding and high surf on Thanksgiving Day, and warned of “major” impacts from coastal flooding on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday. Compared with the Oct. 27 coastal flooding — which damaged 114 homes and other structures in Huntington Beach alone, and also hit Newport Beach hard — this week’s flooding may be worse, forecasters warned. “It’ll most likely be at least as bad as that, and it could be a little worse because we are actually expecting a little bit of higher surf,” said Philip Gonsalves, meteorologist with the weather service office in San Diego, which also issues forecasts for Orange County. Makenna Cassidy and her husband, Jared, far left, join Otto Brown trying to bail out floodwater from their garage in the Sunset Beach area of Huntington Beach on Oct. 27. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times) With the maximum sea level possibly exceeding 8 feet on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day, “this will bring widespread moderate-to-major coastal flooding,” the weather service’s San Diego office said. Newport Beach has been working to temporarily raise seawalls and build sand berms on beaches to prepare. Huntington Beach warned that low-lying roads will be closed Monday through Friday from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. daily, including a total closure of a 3.7-mile stretch of Pacific Coast Highway through the neighborhood of Sunset Beach — from Seal Beach Boulevard to Warner Avenue. Huntington Beach also asked boaters to limit unnecessary travel through Huntington Harbour, since boat wakes — when tides are high — can “cause water to overtop seawalls and bulkheads, potentially flooding neighboring properties and damaging docks and private property.” In Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties, there’s high confidence in record-breaking high tides, the weather service office in Oxnard said. The coastal flooding risk will be the highest on Wednesday and Thursday, exacerbated by elevated-to-high surf that peaks on those two days. With a swell coming from the west, west-facing beaches are at high risk, including the L.A. County coast from Santa Monica to the Palos Verdes Peninsula and the Ventura County coast from Faria Beach to Silver Strand Beach, including the inside of the harbors and Ventura Pier, according to meteorologist Dave Gomberg of the weather service’s Oxnard office. The swell won’t be as big in the Long Beach area, Gomberg said, but he’s still concerned about the high maximum sea levels for the area. Crews have been adding sand to the shoreline of the Long Beach Peninsula, which was hit hard by swells from the south from hurricanes Marie and Rachel. “Visiting beaches is not advised,” especially on Wednesday and Thursday, the weather service’s Oxnard office said, despite how tempting that might be on Thanksgiving, with air temperatures in Southern California forecast to be in the 70s. The shoreline “will be very wet at high tide. Sneaker waves are possible and occur without warning, washing much farther up the beach than expected,” the office said . Sand is added to the Long Beach Peninsula shoreline Oct. 26. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times) On the Central Coast, areas of greatest concern include Morro Bay, Pismo Beach, Oceano Dunes, Cayuco Pier, Avila Beach Pier and Pismo Beach Pier. Maximum sea level records could be broken yet again. On Oct. 27, the tide gauge in San Pedro broke a record, with the maximum sea level reaching 8.19 feet. A reasonable worst-case scenario for the maximum sea level on Wednesday in L.A. County would be up to 8.7 feet, the weather service said. The flooding that came in late October occurred even though there wasn’t significant surf. This time around, “we’ve got some larger surf,” which can worsen coastal flooding, said meteorologist Lisa Phillips of the National Weather Service in Oxnard. But there is some uncertainty. One factor that could result in lower-than-expected sea levels on Thanksgiving Day would be higher pressure moving over the area, which would “kind of squish the water down and may contribute to slightly lower levels of those tides,” weather service meteorologist Bryan Lewis said. Forecasters warned Sunday that the coastal threat could continue after this week. Another swell could threaten the Southern California coast starting again on the Sunday after Thanksgiving.
